title: Interview set-up; family background; move from Nebraska to St. Maries
description: Gale Anderson opens with consent remarks for the interview in St. Maries, Idaho. Elizabeth Haller-Curtis then discusses her family origins, her mother Cora Rose and her father, a jeweler and watchmaker, and how the family traveled by train from Holbrook, Nebraska, to Idaho.

title: Schooling and college; teaching career beginnings
description: She talks about attending St. Maries High School, working her way through college, and borrowing money to finish her degree while teaching. She recalls her first teaching positions, including at Newport, Washington, where she taught grades and music and played instruments in the band.

title: Childhood memories; move up the river; sister and teaching
description: Elizabeth recalls early memories including a trip to Seattle and time in Hawaii, childhood games and school days, and the family's move up the river. She describes her sister's teaching career, their first trip away together, and her own love of music and playing the pipe organ at the Front Row Theater.

title: Family home; changes in the town and its children
description: She reflects on the family home by the river, the deaths of her parents, and how the town and its schoolchildren changed over her first years there. She notes differences in parents' education and how eager the earlier children were to learn.

title: Meeting her husband; marriage; community life
description: Elizabeth tells how she met her husband, who came to St. Maries after World War II and worked as county agent, at the local bowling alley. She describes how the community was anxious for her to marry, how people long knew her by her maiden name, and the family's happy life together.

title: European tour with her sister
description: She recounts a 30-day American Express tour of Europe in 1973 with her sister, from London and Stonehenge to Amsterdam, the Rhine and beyond. The highlight was meeting her sister's French pen pal of 50 years, riding a narrow gauge train through the Alps, being welcomed into a French home, and stopping the tour bus to see her again.

title: Teaching during the war years; school administration work
description: Elizabeth describes teaching from 1939 to 1948 through the war years, when the town was mostly women, children and old men and many mothers worked in factories. She explains her administrative duties, doing bookkeeping for the school district and its trustees and mentoring young teachers.

title: Educational films for rural schools
description: She describes borrowing educational films from the university and scheduling them around the country schools' teaching units. She explains how she helped teachers prepare their classes so the short films would hold the children's attention.

title: Calculators, phonics and math machines in the classroom
description: Elizabeth discusses classroom teaching aids, including hand calculators and whether children still learn the math behind them. She describes a phonics flash card machine that recorded students reading words and a math device with on-screen problems that made arithmetic fun.

title: Teaching experiences; marriage and fire seasons
description: Gale Anderson discusses her teaching career, field trips with students, and her decision to marry. She explains that she and her husband delayed their wedding until after fire season ended and describes adjusting to married life and his subsequent illness.

title: Lookout life; isolation; hobbies
description: Anderson describes living at a remote fire lookout station without electricity or plumbing, her bird watching activities, and her preference for solitary hobbies. She reflects on her independent nature and visits to Washington, DC for Eisenhower's inauguration.

title: Rural living; pros and cons
description: The conversation turns to the advantages and disadvantages of small-town life, including cheaper living costs, helpful neighbors, and limited shopping. Anderson also mentions her love of gardening and watching television programs.

title: Retirement activities; Depression era teaching
description: Anderson describes her current retirement activities including golf, travel, and the Lady's Country Club. She recalls teaching during the Depression when staff took pay cuts to avoid layoffs and discusses her husband's determination during his illness.

title: Working mothers; parental involvement; fatherhood absence
description: Anderson shares her belief that mothers should stay home with young children rather than work, describing behavioral differences in students. She also discusses her own mother's influence and notes the lack of father participation in school activities throughout her career.

title: Teaching reflections; gender discrimination
description: The interview concludes with Anderson reflecting on the rewards of teaching and addressing gender discrimination in education. She discusses unequal pay scales for women teachers compared to men and discriminatory practices regarding coaching stipends and qualifications.

title: Red Cross flood relief; long hours at St. Maries
description: Gale Anderson describes her exhausting schedule doing Red Cross disaster work during a flood near St. Maries, driving back and forth and sleeping only a few hours at a time, often in her car. She recalls the trauma for the site director and the dedication of the volunteers she worked with.

title: Flood response operations; rising water
description: She explains how she monitored the rising water with the sheriff's office and stayed three weeks at an office set up in the Department of Health and Welfare. She points out landmarks flooded below her house and describes the Red Cross operation, including emergency mass care and later individual case work for displaced families.

title: Advantages of rural living; wildlife
description: Asked about rural life, Gale says she sees no disadvantages, valuing solitude, freedom, animals, and raising three children outside town. She describes watching deer, bobcats, and ospreys from her home and her belief that natural resources are for people's use without waste.

title: Recreation; television and reading
description: Gale talks about enjoying television, especially history and wildlife programs, and preferring suspenseful and historical novels to magazines. She counts her volunteer work as part of her recreation and change of pace.

title: Childbirth; teaching children about life
description: She recalls the births of her children, including a long labor and later operations, and mentions her father delivering her older brother and Doctor Shunk delivering siblings. Growing up with many farm animals, she learned about reproduction naturally and answered her children's questions the same practical way.

title: Family size; children and grandchildren
description: Gale explains she had three children and was content, having suffered blood clots and surgeries, and that she enjoys children once they are past infancy. She describes encouraging her children to attend college, discouraging early marriage, and supporting their changing majors.

title: Education and career changes
description: She recounts wanting to join the Army Nurse Corps during World War II, working for her father, studying agriculture at university, and dropping a teaching path after disliking an education class. She later used her agriculture training at home, in extension work, and in developing recipes to manage her children's food allergies.

title: Church and religious beliefs
description: Gale identifies as Catholic, describes a religiously mixed family including Mormon, Protestant, and evangelist relatives, and says her children read the Bible. She explains that she stopped taking her children to Sunday school because she saw church literature as promoting one-world government, which clashed with her independent views.

title: Welfare views; run for office
description: She supports assistance only for the genuinely handicapped and needy, recalling her poor upbringing when welfare carried shame. She mentions running as the first woman from Benewah County for state representative and deciding she could accomplish more working from outside the legislature.

title: Women's equality; marriage partnership
description: Gale says she does not compete with men but believes women should achieve their full potential and be recognized, while accepting those who choose homemaking. She describes a marriage in which her husband supported her absences, cared for the children, and shares decisions with her as an equal.

title: Shared interests; encouraging her husband's writing
description: She discusses conversations with her husband about business, stocks, livestock, and community roles, noting he chaired the school board. She encourages him to write about his southern Oregon family, who built covered bridges in Jackson County, and picks up books for him in her travels.

title: Writing plans; Native American history and youth project
description: Gale outlines her plans for children's books, including one about a pet deer illustrated by her daughter and another weaving in Native American life with help from her artist sister. She describes her friendship with the local tribe, disaster work for them in 1964, a tribal council visit, and a project to teach Indian youth about government, reflecting on prejudice and the reservation's reduction from 300,000 to 79,000 acres.

title: Indian land claims; property rights and state agreements; prejudice and economics
description: Gale Anderson discusses a proposed settlement with Missouri Indians regarding 600,000 acres of Hafer Park in Idaho, addressing questions of property rights, treaty obligations, and state jurisdiction. She distinguishes between personal and economic prejudice while defending both Indian rights and individual property rights.

title: Government bureaucracy; threats to local control; defending individual rights
description: Anderson describes herself as a pragmatic humanitarian who aggressively defends her rights and feels threatened by excessive government, particularly unelected committees and commissions. She criticizes these bodies for replacing legislative action and argues that local government, however flawed, is more responsive than federal agencies.

title: Rural school conditions; independent learning; advantages of small schools
description: Anderson recalls her experience teaching in rural schools with low salaries and limited instructional time, noting that students learned to study independently and help one another. She discusses how these children performed well on achievement tests despite the challenges, and describes parental concerns about school elimination.

title: School consolidation; county economics and final decisions
description: She explains her support for consolidating small schools due to the county's limited tax base, poor land distribution, and inability to afford adequate salaries or facilities. She describes the final arrangements for consolidation and her departure from the district before the merger was completed.
